questions.stem: In the nuclear model of the atom, what holds the electrons in their energy levels around the nucleus?
options: Magnetic attraction between neighbouring electrons in a shell
Strong nuclear force acting between electrons and the nucleus
Electrostatic attraction between the electrons and the protons
Gravitational attraction between the electrons and the neutrons
questions.explanation: Electrons are negative and protons are positive, so the electrons are held by electrostatic attraction to the nucleus. Neutrons have no charge, and gravity between such small masses is far too weak to matter.

questions.stem: What is the electron shell arrangement of a sodium atom (atomic number 11)?
questions.explanation: The first shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons and the second 8, leaving 1 electron in the third shell. The arrangement 2, 8, 8, 1 belongs to potassium, which has 19 electrons.

questions.stem: Which element has the electron shell arrangement 2, 8, 6?
options: Silicon
Argon
Sulfur
Oxygen
questions.explanation: Adding the electrons gives 2 + 8 + 6 = 16, the atomic number of sulfur. Oxygen is 2, 6, with 6 outer electrons but only two shells.

questions.stem: What is the electron shell arrangement of a calcium atom (atomic number 20)?
questions.explanation: For elements 1 to 20 the third shell takes 8 electrons before the fourth shell starts filling, so calcium's 20 electrons are arranged 2, 8, 8, 2. Putting 10 in the third shell ignores this rule for the first 20 elements.

questions.stem: An atom has three occupied shells and 5 electrons in its outer shell. Which statement about it is correct?
options: It is phosphorus, in period 3 and group 15
It is nitrogen, in period 2 and group 15
It is boron, in period 3 and group 13
It is aluminium, in period 5 and group 13
questions.explanation: The number of occupied shells gives the period and the outer-shell electrons give the group, so the atom is 2, 8, 5, which is phosphorus (atomic number 15). Nitrogen has the same outer electrons but only two shells.

questions.stem: Element X is in period 2 and has the same number of outer-shell electrons as chlorine. What is its atomic number?
questions.explanation: Chlorine is 2, 8, 7, so X also has 7 outer electrons. In period 2 that gives 2, 7, a total of 9 electrons, which is fluorine.

questions.stem: Why do the elements of group 2 form ions with a 2+ charge?
options: Their atoms share two electrons with another atom to form a bond
Their atoms lose their two outer-shell electrons to leave a full outer shell
Their atoms gain two electrons to fill their outer shell completely
Their atoms lose two protons from the nucleus to become stable
questions.explanation: A group 2 atom has 2 outer electrons and loses them, leaving a full shell beneath with 2 more protons than electrons. Gaining electrons would give a negative ion, and protons are never lost in chemical reactions.

questions.stem: What is the charge on a stable ion of nitrogen?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is 2, 5, so it gains 3 electrons to reach a full outer shell of 8, giving N³⁻. Losing 5 electrons would take far more energy than gaining 3.

questions.stem: Which particle has the electron arrangement 2, 8, 8?
options: A sodium ion, Na⁺
A magnesium ion, Mg²⁺
A fluoride ion, F⁻
A sulfide ion, S²⁻
questions.explanation: Sulfur (16 electrons) gains 2 to give 18 electrons, arranged 2, 8, 8. Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and F⁻ each have 10 electrons, arranged 2, 8.

questions.stem: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in the ion ⁴⁰Ca²⁺ (atomic number 20)?
options: 20 protons, 20 neutrons and 18 electrons
20 protons, 20 neutrons and 22 electrons
20 protons, 40 neutrons and 18 electrons
18 protons, 20 neutrons and 20 electrons
questions.explanation: The atomic number gives 20 protons and the mass number 40 gives 40 − 20 = 20 neutrons. A 2+ charge means 2 fewer electrons than protons, so 18; a positive ion has lost electrons, not gained them.

questions.stem: Elements X and Y have shell arrangements 2, 8, 2 and 2, 7. What is the formula of the compound they form?
options: XY₂
X₂Y
XY
X₂Y₇
questions.explanation: X is magnesium, forming X²⁺, and Y is fluorine, forming Y⁻. Two Y⁻ ions balance one X²⁺, so the formula is XY₂; X₂Y would have the charges the wrong way round.

questions.stem: An ion X²⁻ has 18 electrons and 18 neutrons. What is the mass number of this isotope of X?
questions.explanation: A 2− ion has 2 more electrons than protons, so X has 18 − 2 = 16 protons (sulfur). Mass number = protons + neutrons = 16 + 18 = 34; adding electrons and neutrons gives the wrong value of 36.

questions.stem: What do the isotopes carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 have in common?
options: The same number of neutrons in the nucleus
The same mass number for every atom
The same mass for one mole of atoms
The same number of protons in the nucleus
questions.explanation: Isotopes are atoms of one element, so they have the same number of protons (6 for carbon) but different numbers of neutrons. That difference in neutrons gives them different mass numbers and molar masses.

questions.stem: How many neutrons are in an atom of ³⁷Cl (atomic number 17)?
questions.explanation: The number of neutrons is the mass number minus the atomic number: 37 − 17 = 20. The mass number 37 counts protons and neutrons together.

questions.stem: Why do isotopes of the same element have the same chemical properties?
options: They have the same density and the same melting point
They have the same number and arrangement of electrons
They have the same number of neutrons in the nucleus
They have the same mass, so they react at the same rate
questions.explanation: Chemical reactions involve the electrons, and isotopes of an element have the same electron configuration. They differ in neutrons, which changes their mass and physical properties but not how they bond.

questions.stem: Which property is most likely to differ between water made with hydrogen-1 and water made with hydrogen-2 (deuterium)?
options: The number of electrons in each molecule
The density of the liquid
The shape of each water molecule
The type of bonds within each molecule
questions.explanation: Deuterium has an extra neutron, so heavy water molecules are heavier and the liquid is denser. The bonding, molecular shape and electron count are the same, because isotopes have the same electron configuration.

questions.stem: Which pair of atoms are isotopes of each other?
options: An atom with 8 protons and 8 neutrons, and one with 8 protons and 10 neutrons
An atom with 8 protons and 8 neutrons, and one with 7 protons and 8 neutrons
An atom with 6 protons and 8 neutrons, and one with 7 protons and 7 neutrons
An atom with 18 protons and 22 neutrons, and one with 20 protons and 20 neutrons
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, which is true only of the two oxygen atoms with 8 protons. Atoms with the same mass number but different proton numbers, such as carbon-14 and nitrogen-14, are different elements.

questions.stem: Relative atomic mass is defined relative to which standard?
options: One sixteenth of the mass of an atom of oxygen-16
The mass of one proton plus one electron
One twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12
The mass of one atom of hydrogen-1
questions.explanation: The relative atomic mass of an element is the weighted average mass of its atoms compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. Carbon-12 is the agreed standard, so it has a relative isotopic mass of exactly 12.

questions.stem: What information about an element does a mass spectrum provide?
options: The isotopes present and their relative abundances
The number of electrons in each energy level
The melting points of each of its isotopes
The number of bonds each atom can form
questions.explanation: A mass spectrum shows a peak for each isotope at its mass-to-charge ratio, and the height of each peak shows its relative abundance. From these the relative atomic mass can be calculated.

questions.stem: In a mass spectrometer, how are the ions of different isotopes separated?
options: By heating them until each isotope boils off
By filtering them through a semipermeable membrane
By deflecting the ions with a magnetic field
By dissolving them in solvents of different polarity
questions.explanation: The sample is ionised and the ions are deflected by a magnetic field, with lighter ions deflected more than heavier ones of the same charge. Boiling and dissolving cannot separate isotopes, because isotopes behave almost identically in those processes.

questions.stem: Boron has two isotopes: boron-10 (20%) and boron-11 (80%). What is the relative atomic mass of boron?
questions.explanation: Weighted average = (10 × 20 + 11 × 80)/100 = 10.8. A simple average of 10 and 11 gives 10.5, which ignores that boron-11 is four times as common.

questions.stem: A simplified mass spectrum of neon shows two peaks: m/z 20 with relative height 9.0 and m/z 22 with relative height 1.0. What is the relative atomic mass of neon from this spectrum?
questions.explanation: Weighted average = (20 × 9.0 + 22 × 1.0)/(9.0 + 1.0) = 202/10 = 20.2. An answer of 21.0 is the unweighted average of the two mass numbers.

questions.stem: A mass spectrum of chlorine shows peaks at m/z 35 and 37 with relative heights 6 and 2. What is the relative atomic mass of chlorine?
questions.explanation: The heights give 6/8 = 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37. (35 × 6 + 37 × 2)/8 = 284/8 = 35.5; 36.0 is the simple average.

questions.stem: Magnesium is 79% magnesium-24, 10% magnesium-25 and 11% magnesium-26. What is its relative atomic mass, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: (24 × 79 + 25 × 10 + 26 × 11)/100 = (1896 + 250 + 286)/100 = 24.32. The value sits close to 24 because magnesium-24 is by far the most abundant isotope.

questions.stem: Element Q has two isotopes, ⁶³Q and ⁶⁵Q, and a relative atomic mass of 63.6. Taking each isotope's mass as its mass number, what percentage of Q atoms are ⁶³Q?
questions.explanation: Let x be the fraction of ⁶³Q: 63x + 65(1 − x) = 63.6, so 2x = 1.4 and x = 0.70. The relative atomic mass is closer to 63, so the lighter isotope must be the more abundant one, which rules out 30%.

questions.stem: Element Z has isotopes ⁶⁹Z (60.0%) and ⁷¹Z (40.0%). A student calculates its relative atomic mass as 70.0. What mistake did the student make?
options: They took a simple average instead of weighting by abundance
They swapped the abundances of the two isotopes
They added the mass numbers instead of averaging them
They used the atomic number instead of the mass number
questions.explanation: 70.0 is the midpoint of 69 and 71, a simple average. The weighted value is (69 × 60.0 + 71 × 40.0)/100 = 69.8; swapping the abundances would give 70.2.

questions.stem: Why is the relative atomic mass of chlorine 35.5 even though no chlorine atom has a mass of 35.5?
options: It is measured relative to hydrogen, which makes every value a little larger
It is a weighted average of the masses of chlorine's naturally occurring isotopes
It includes the mass of the electrons, which adds half a mass unit to each atom
Chlorine atoms lose half a neutron when they are ionised in a mass spectrometer
questions.explanation: Natural chlorine is a mixture of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37, and the relative atomic mass averages their masses weighted by abundance. Electrons are far too light to add half a unit, and the standard is carbon-12, not hydrogen.

questions.stem: Moving from sodium to chlorine along period 3, what happens to the size of the atoms?
options: It decreases
It increases
It stays the same
It increases, then decreases
questions.explanation: Across a period the number of protons increases while the electrons are added to the same outer shell. The greater nuclear charge pulls the outer shell closer, so the atoms get smaller.

questions.stem: Lithium, sodium and potassium atoms get larger down group 1. What is the main reason?
options: Each element has an extra occupied electron shell
Each element has fewer protons attracting its electrons
The outer electrons are shared with more neighbours
The nucleus repels the outer electrons more strongly
questions.explanation: Lithium has 2 shells, sodium 3 and potassium 4, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus each time. The number of protons actually increases down the group, but the extra shells outweigh it.

questions.stem: The valency of an element is the number of bonds its atoms can form. What is the valency of silicon (2, 8, 4)?
questions.explanation: Silicon has 4 outer electrons, so it shares 4 electrons to complete its outer shell and forms 4 bonds. Valency rises from 1 to 4 across period 3 from sodium to silicon, then falls back to 1 at chlorine.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly gives the valencies of the period 3 elements Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar in order?
questions.explanation: Metals lose their outer electrons (1, 2, 3), silicon shares 4, and the non-metals need 3, 2 and 1 more electrons to complete the shell. Argon already has a full shell, so its valency is 0.

questions.stem: Which property is typical of non-metals?
options: Malleability, so they can be hammered flat
Forming positive ions in reactions
Poor conduction of heat and electricity
Shiny surfaces that can be polished
questions.explanation: Most non-metals are poor conductors and are brittle or gaseous. Lustre, malleability and forming positive ions are properties of metals.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the elements of group 18?
options: They are soft metals that form 2+ ions
They are unreactive gases whose atoms have full outer shells
They are reactive metals that form 1+ ions in water
They are coloured non-metals that form 1− ions
questions.explanation: Group 18 (the noble gases) have full outer shells, so they rarely react and exist as single atoms. Forming 1− ions describes group 17, and forming 1+ ions describes group 1.

questions.stem: Lithium, sodium and potassium are each added to water. How does the reaction change down group 1?
options: It becomes more vigorous, because the outer electron is lost more easily
It becomes less vigorous, because the atoms have more protons
It becomes more vigorous, because the atoms gain electrons more easily
It stays the same, because each atom has one outer electron
questions.explanation: Down the group the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily and reactivity increases. Group 1 metals react by losing an electron, not gaining one.

questions.stem: How does the reactivity of the halogens change down group 17, and why?
options: It decreases, because the larger atoms have fewer outer-shell electrons
It increases, because the larger atoms have a greater nuclear charge
It decreases, because the larger atoms attract an extra electron less strongly
It increases, because the larger atoms lose their outer electrons more easily
questions.explanation: Halogens react by gaining an electron. Down the group the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so an incoming electron is attracted less strongly and fluorine is the most reactive. Every halogen has 7 outer electrons.

questions.stem: Chlorine water is added to a colourless solution of potassium bromide and the solution turns orange-brown as bromine forms. What does this show?
options: Chlorine and bromine have the same reactivity because both are in group 17
Chlorine is more reactive than bromine and displaces it from its compound
Bromine is more reactive than chlorine and displaces it from its compound
Potassium is more reactive than chlorine and gives up its electron to it
questions.explanation: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂: chlorine gains electrons from bromide ions, so chlorine is the more reactive halogen. This fits the trend of halogen reactivity decreasing down the group.

questions.stem: Across period 3, sodium reacts vigorously with water, magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water and aluminium barely reacts. Which explanation fits this trend?
options: More protons and more outer electrons to lose make it harder for each atom to form its ion
The atoms get larger across the period, so their outer electrons are held more loosely
The atoms have more electron shells across the period, which shields the outer electrons
The metals become non-metals across the period and so gain electrons instead
questions.explanation: Across the period the nuclear charge rises while the outer electrons stay in the same shell, and more electrons must be lost, so the metals react less readily. The atoms get smaller across the period, not larger, and all three have three shells.

questions.stem: An unknown element is a dull yellow solid that shatters when struck and does not conduct electricity. Where in the periodic table is it most likely found?
options: On the left of the table, among the group 1 metals
In the middle of the table, among the transition metals
At the far right of the table, in group 18
On the right of the table, among the non-metals
questions.explanation: Dullness, brittleness and non-conduction are non-metal properties, and non-metals are on the right of the periodic table (sulfur fits this description). Group 18 elements are gases, not solids, at room temperature.
